summary:
Querétaro de Arteaga stands under the national framework of Mexico, where legal gender recognition remains the central unfinished task of equality law. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure, and its state-by-state table lists Querétaro among the six states that have never legislated any such procedure. A trans visitor to Querétaro therefore has no local administrative route to align identity documents with lived identity; the papers carried on arrival are the only identification available, and they cannot be corrected there.

Where recognition is absent, mismatched documents are the documented exposure. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that delays and refusals in Tabasco leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police, and it presents Tabasco as the clearest case among the six states whose legislatures still refuse any procedure. The same report set those barriers against killings, including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Querétaro's Penal Code cuts the other way on one specific point. The reform prohibiting Esfuerzos para Corregir la Orientación Sexual y la Identidad de Género (ECOSIG), commonly called conversion therapies, was published and is in force as of reporting on 20 September 2023, and it sets two to six years' imprisonment, a fine of 20 to 2,000 times the UMA and 50 to 100 hours of community service, treating such practices as discriminatory and torturous under articles 1 and 6 of the Inter-American Convention to Prevent and Punish Torture.
tangentialFactors:
Violence against trans people across Mexico intensified over the year to mid-2024. AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, with the killings drawing LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100.

One legislature has moved to close a specific gap. Mexico City's Congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide; the statute takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists describe the law as critical to their sense of safety. Querétaro has not adopted comparable legislation.

Inter-American authorities have pressed the same point. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels.

The gap between statute and practice is the recurring finding. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice; the analysis explicitly cautions that its earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture. Human Rights Watch's 31 March 2025 backgrounder likewise calls on the states that lack recognition procedures to adopt them and warns that implementation differs sharply from one state to another.

Partnership recognition is settled at the national level: same-sex marriage has been legal across Mexico since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.
localsOnly:
Residents of Querétaro who need a name or gender marker change have no state procedure to apply to, since the state has never legislated one; the practical consequence documented elsewhere in Mexico is carrying identity documents that contradict lived identity. Human Rights Watch's Tabasco research was co-authored with a local trans community organisation, and the organization frames Tabasco as the clearest instance of a legislature refusing any procedure.

The conversion-practice ban is resident-facing protection with real penalties attached. Walter López, spokesman for the Frente Queretano por el Derecho a la No Discriminación, described the published reform as a milestone compared with states where a comparable ban remains unpublished, while stating that a first generation of LGBTIQ+ reforms is still pending in the state congress.

Same-sex marriage has been available nationwide since 2009, so partnership recognition does not depend on Querétaro's own legislation.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Querétaro-specific incident, arrest, prosecution or court decision under the conversion-practice ban was identified in the available sources; the ban's enforcement record in the state is unresolved rather than documented as active or dormant.

The inventory contains no Querétaro-specific figures for violence against trans people. The national counts cited here come from Transgender Europe, AP and Agencia Presentes and cannot be attributed to this state.

Whether Querétaro's administrative bodies or courts have any unpublished practice for changing gender markers, despite the absence of legislation, is not addressed by these sources and remains unresolved.

The pending legislative reforms referred to by local advocates are not itemised in the sources, so their subject matter and status are unresolved.
